name: Single-bishop ending — good bishop against bad

plans.label: Fix their pawns on their bishop's colour
plans.description: Fix the opponent's pawns on the squares their own bishop moves on, and keep yours off your bishop's colour: their bishop becomes a tall pawn chained to targets, yours keeps every option.

success.note: The pawn-and-bishop colour complex is not in the shipped vocabulary.

plans.label: Invade on the colour the bad bishop cannot touch
plans.description: March the king in along the squares the bad bishop can never defend; the break-in happens on one colour complex and the defender's bishop watches it from the other.

success.note: Colour complexes and king routes are outside this vocabulary.

plans.label: Spend the spare tempo
plans.description: A good bishop has waiting moves along free diagonals that the bad bishop lacks; in a fixed position, hand the move over and let zugzwang force the concession the direct approach could not.

success.note: Zugzwang is a to-move property no static census expresses.

plans.label: Free the bad bishop or trade it
plans.description: Either get the pawns off the bishop's colour while there is still time, or trade the bad bishop — even at a visible structural price; the piece that cannot move is worth less than the pawn structure it costs to release.

success.note: Holding is an outcome and has no structural signature here.

plans.label: Bishop outside the chain
plans.description: A bad bishop standing in front of its own pawn chain is a different piece from one buried behind it: activate it to the outside before the position fixes, even at the cost of a tempo or a weakness.

success.note: Inside-versus-outside the chain is geometry the vocabulary cannot express.

watch: One bishop each is all the trigger can see: the vocabulary has no square-colour predicate, so same-coloured and opposite-coloured bishop endings — different universes — both fire here. Check the bishops' colours; if they differ, use the opposite-coloured-bishops entry instead.
Which bishop is 'bad' lives in the pawn-colour complex, also outside the vocabulary; the trigger names the census, the diagnosis is yours.
Colour convention: White is authored as the stronger/attacking side. Mirror the plans when the colours are reversed; the trigger fires only for the White-side census.
typicalMistakes: Fixing your own pawns on your bishop's colour for one move of convenience — the structure outlives the tempo.
Refusing the bad-bishop trade when it was offered cheaply, then losing to the zugzwang the trade would have prevented.
Winning the bishop battle but losing the pawn ending: count the king-and-pawn ending before the last trade, because good-versus-bad evaporates the moment the bishops leave.

sources: Family per design/04-content-architecture.md section 4 (minor piece: good/bad bishop).
Tablebase honesty: typical positions of this family exceed seven pieces; no tablebase ground truth exists for them and none was consulted.
UNGROUNDED: plan, watch, and mistake prose is authored endgame-literature consensus rendered by the author; no engine or tablebase has graded any claim in this entry.

Trigger gap: bishop square colour is inexpressible, so this trigger cannot be told apart from the opposite-coloured-bishops census; both entries fire on the same positions and each names the other. This is the sharpest known gap in the shipped vocabulary for endgame families.
